children: Activity in Canada's services industry continued to weaken last month as uncertainty was still weighing on confidence and sales, data released Thursday showed.

The S&P Global Canada services purchasing managers index declined to 46.8 in August, in what was the sharpest retreat since February. The index has for three months signaled a contraction in the services sector, remaining below the 50 breakeven mark after nudging up to 49.1 in July.
Services activity and new business volumes were down in August, and by greater degree than in the prior month and input price inflation remained elevated despite easing.

"Against the backdrop of escalating trade tensions with the U.S. and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, the underlying health of Canada's service sector continued to suffer," Paul Smith, economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said.

Smith said that services companies noted a challenging business environment characterized by uncertainty and a lack of willingness amongst clients to commit to new contracts, with those surveyed pointing to tariffs and trade tensions as well as the Iran war that continues to spur volatility in energy costs.
Confidence among services providers regarding the 12-month outlook fell to  its lowest level since June 2025, S&P Global's survey found.

Elevated prices are a concern for companies going forward, S&P Global said, adding that anecdotal evidence from the survey indicated rising energy and fuel prices again underpinned an increase in overall costs during August. Higher wage expenses were also reported.

Total cost inflation remained elevated and above trend in the latest month, despite falling since July. Although service providers want to pass on higher input costs to clients through an increase in charges, competitive pressures and weak demand are limiting pricing power and so overall output inflation softened to the lowest since March, S&P Global said.

There was little change in industry employment in August, after two months of modest growth. The survey found that several services companies sought to keep on top of workloads by hiring additional workers, but there were instances of job-leavers not being replaced and several reports of companies finding it difficult to recruit suitable staff.

Manufacturing activity in Canada weakened slightly last month but for a fifth straight month was in expansion territory. S&P Global's Canadian manufacturing PMI index slipped to 53 in August from 53.5 a month prior.

Canada's economy emerged from the second quarter on solid footing, though risks are elevated as fuel prices remain high and the U.S. introduced fresh tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. The economy grew at an annualized rate of 3.3% in the latest quarter, the strongest expansion since the start of 2023 and a pickup from modest growth of 0.3% in the first quarter of this year.
An early estimate of industry-level gross domestic product for July indicates little change from the month before, following three straight months of growth.
